text: The Kernel Trick allows us to featurize a mapping from R^d to R^D, where d represents input features and D represents features after featurization. Degree-p polynomials can blow up to D × (d^p) features. When d and p are not small, this becomes computationally intractable very quickly. For instance, if you have 100 features per feature vector and you want to use degree-4 polynomial decision functions, then each featurized feature vector has a length of roughly 4 million. Today, we can use those features without computing them!

In many learning algorithms, the weights can be expressed as a linear combination of training points, and we can use inner products of φ(x) without needing to compute φ(x) explicitly. Suppose w = X^T a = Σ a_i X_i for some a ∈ R^n. By substituting this identity into the algorithm, we can optimize the dual weights a (also known as dual parameters) instead of D primal weights w.

For Kernel Ridge Regression, we center X and y so their means are zero: X_i = X_i - µ, y_i = y_i - µ, where µ is the mean. This allows us to replace I with I in the normal equations: (X X + λI)w = X y. To kernelize ridge regression, we need the weights to be a linear combination of the training points. This only occurs if we penalize the bias term w = α, as these normal equations do. When we center X and y, the expected value of the bias term is zero.

Suppose a is a solution to (X X + λI)a = y. This always has a solution if λ > 0. Then, X y = X X a + λX a = (X X + λI)X a. Therefore, w = X a is a solution to the normal equations, and w is a linear combination of training points! a is a dual solution that solves the dual form of ridge regression: Find a that minimizes ||X a - y||^2 + λ ||X a||^2.
For training, we solve (X X + λI)a = y for a. For testing, the regression function is h(z) = w^T z = a^T X z, which is a weighted sum of inner products.

Let k(x, z) = x z be a kernel function. Later, we’ll replace x and z with φ(x) and φ(z), and that’s where the magic will happen. Let K = XX be the kernel matrix. Note K = k(X, X). K may be singular. If so, probably no solution if λ = 0. Then we must choose a positive λ. But that’s okay. K is always singular if n > d + 1. But don’t worry about the case n > d + 1, because you would only want to use the dual form when d > n, i.e., for polynomial features. But K could still be singular when d > n.

The dual/kernel ridge regression algorithm involves solving (K + λI)a = y for a in O(n^3) time. For each test point z, we compute h(z) = Σ a_i k(X, z) in O(nd) time per test point. This method does not use X directly! Only k. It is important to note that dual ridge regression produces the same predictions as primal ridge regression (with a penalized bias term). The difference is the running time; the dual algorithm is faster if d > n, because the primal algorithm solves a d x d linear system, whereas the dual algorithm solves an n x n linear system.

The Kernel Trick (aka Kernelization) allows us to compute a polynomial kernel without actually computing the features. The polynomial kernel of degree p is k(x, z) = (x z + 1)^p. Theorem: (x z + 1)^p = φ(x) φ(z) for some φ(x) containing every monomial in x of degree 0...p. For example, for d = 2, p = 2: (x z + 1)^2 = x^2 z^2 + 2xz + 1 = φ(x) φ(z). Notice the factors of p^2. If you try a higher polynomial degree p, you’ll see a wider variety of these constants.

Key insight: compute φ(x) φ(z) in O(d) time instead of O(D) = O(dp), even though φ(x) has length D. Kernel ridge regression replaces X with φ(X): let k(x, z) = φ(x) φ(z), but doesn’t compute φ(x) or φ(z); it computes k(x, z) = (x z + 1)^p. Running times for three ridge algorithms are as follows: primal O(D^3 + D^2n), dual (no kernel trick) O(n^3 + n^2D), kernel O(n^3 + n^2d) for training, and testing per test point O(D), O(nD), O(nd) respectively. This allows us to perform polynomial regression with an exponentially long, high-order polynomial in less time than it would take to write out the final polynomial.

Kernel Logistic Regression involves using a design matrix D with rows corresponding to the featurized training points. The algorithm starts with an arbitrary weight vector w_0 and iteratively updates it until convergence. The update rule is given by w = w + ε(X)(y - s(Xw)), where s is applied component-wise to the vector (Xw). For each test point z, the hypothesis h(z) is computed as h(z) = s(w^T(z)). The dual formulation uses weights a, initialized to zero, and the kernel matrix K = (X)(X). The update rule for the dual weights is a = a + ε(y - s(Ka)), which has the same effect as the primal update.

In dual/kernel logistic regression, the running time depends on the original dimension d rather than the length D of the feature map. The training times for different methods are as follows: Primal: O(nDj) time, Dual (no kernel trick): O(n^2D + n^2j) time, and Kernel: O(n^2d + n^2j) time. An alternative training method is stochastic gradient descent (SGD), where the primal logistic SGD step is w = w + εy - s(Xw)X. The dual logistic SGD maintains a vector q = Ka, where q_i = (X_i)^T w.

In the dual formulation, the algorithm initializes a = 0 and q = 0, and iterates until convergence. A random index i is chosen from the training set, and the update for the dual weight is a = a + ε(y - s(q)), which takes O(1) time. The vector q is updated as q = q + ε(y - s(q))K, which computes q = Ka in O(n) time, avoiding the O(n^2) time of quadratic matrix-vector multiplication. This efficiency is a significant advantage of the dual formulation.

For testing, if the number of training points and test points both exceed D/d, classifying with primal weights w may be faster. The weight vector is computed as w = (X)a in O(nD) time (once only). For each test point z, the hypothesis h(z) is computed as h(z) = s(w^T(z)), which takes O(D) time per test point.

The Gaussian kernel, also known as a radial basis function kernel, is defined as k(x, z) = exp(-||x - z||^2). This kernel takes O(d) time to compute, where d is the dimensionality of the input space. The idea behind using the Gaussian kernel is to perform computations in an infinite-dimensional space, which allows for more complex feature representations.

For a single input feature per sample point, the feature vector that corresponds to the Gaussian kernel can be expressed as φ(x) = (exp(-x^2/2), exp(-x^2/2), ...). This results in an infinite vector, and the series φ(x) · φ(z) converges to k(x, z). However, in practice, this infinite-dimensional representation is not used directly; instead, the kernel function k(., .) is utilized.

It is important to note that when working with high-dimensional spaces, it is often more useful to think of the kernel k as a measure of similarity between two points rather than trying to visualize the points themselves. A key observation is that the hypothesis h(z) = Σ a_j k(X_j, z) is a linear combination of Gaussians centered at the training points, where the dual weights a_j are the coefficients of this linear combination.

In the context of ridge regression with a Gaussian kernel, the resulting regression model can be visualized as a linear combination of Gaussians centered at the training points. This means that the model can effectively capture complex relationships in the data by leveraging the properties of the Gaussian kernel.

The Kernel Trick is very popular in practice for several reasons. It provides a very smooth function; in fact, it is infinitely differentiable and C∞-continuous. It behaves somewhat like k-nearest neighbors but is smoother and oscillates less than polynomials, depending on the choice of the kernel. The kernel k(x, z) is interpreted as a similarity measure, being maximum when z = x and approaching zero as the distance increases. Training points "vote" for the value at z, with closer points receiving a weightier vote. The standard kernel k(x, z) = x^T z assigns more weight to training point vectors that point in roughly the same direction as z. In contrast, the Gaussian kernel assigns more weight to training points near z. The choice of kernel should be made by validation.

The choice of the kernel trades off bias versus variance. A larger bandwidth parameter (σ) results in wider Gaussians and a smoother function, which introduces more bias and less variance. Conversely, a smaller σ leads to narrower Gaussians, resulting in less bias and more variance. This trade-off is crucial in model selection, as it affects the model's ability to generalize to unseen data.

There are many other kernels defined directly as kernel functions without worrying about the specific feature space. However, not every function can be a kernel function. A function qualifies as a kernel only if it always generates a positive semidefinite kernel matrix for every sample. There is an elaborate theory about how to construct valid kernel functions, but you probably won’t need it. The polynomial and Gaussian kernels are the two most popular by far.

Be aware that not every featurization leads to a kernel function that can be computed faster than O(D) time. In fact, the vast majority cannot. Featurizations that can are rare and special. Understanding the limitations of kernel functions and their computational efficiency is essential for effective model building.

Neural networks can both classification and regression. They tie together several ideas from the course: perceptrons, linear regression, logistic regression, ensembles of learners, and stochastic gradient descent. They also incorporate the idea of lifting sample points to a higher-dimensional feature space, but with a new twist: neural nets can learn features themselves.

I want to begin by reminding you of the story I told you at the beginning of the semester, about Frank Rosenblatt’s invention of perceptrons in 1957. Remember that he held a press conference where he predicted that perceptrons would be 'the embryo of an electronic computer that [the Navy] expects will be able to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence.'

Perceptron research continued until something monumental happened in 1969. Marvin Minsky, one of the founding fathers of AI, and Seymour Papert published a book called "Perceptrons." Part of the book was devoted to things perceptrons can’t do, and one of those things is XOR. Think of the four outputs here as sample points in two-dimensional space. Two of them are in class 1, and two of them are in class 0. We want to find a linear classifier that separates the 1’s from the 0’s. Can we do it? No.

Minsky and Papert were basically saying, "Frank, you’re telling us this machine is going to be conscious of its own existence but it can’t do XOR?" The book had a devastating effect on the field. After its publication, almost no research was done on neural net-like ideas for a decade, a time we now call the "AI Winter." Shortly after the book was published, Frank Rosenblatt died.

One thing I don’t understand is why the book was so fatal when there are several almost obvious ways to get around the XOR problem. Here’s the easiest: if you add one new quadratic feature, x_1 * x_2, XOR is linearly separable in 3D. Now we can find a plane that cuts through the cube obliquely and separates the 0’s from the 1’s.

However, there’s an even more powerful way to do XOR. The idea is to design linear classifiers whose output is the input to other linear classifiers. That way, you should be able to emulate arbitrary logic circuits. Suppose I put together some linear decision functions like this.

If I interpret the output as true if z is greater than one-half or false if z is less than one-half, can I do XOR with this? A linear combination of a linear combination is a linear combination... only works for linearly separable points.

We need one more idea to make neural nets. We need to add some sort of nonlinearity between the linear combinations. Let’s call these boxes that compute linear combinations "neurons." If a neuron sends the linear combination it computes through some nonlinear function before sending it onto other neurons, then the neurons can act somewhat like logic gates.

The traditional choice has been to use the logistic function. The logistic function can’t go below zero or above one, which is nice because it can’t ever get huge and oversaturate the other neurons it’s sending information to. The logistic function is also smooth, which means it has well-defined gradients and Hessians we can use for optimization.
With logistic functions between the linear combinations, here’s a two-level perceptron that computes the XOR function. A natural question is: can an algorithm learn a function like this?

In a neural network with one hidden layer, the input layer consists of features x_1, x_2, ..., x_d, where x_1 = 1 for the bias term. The hidden units are denoted as h_1, h_2, ..., h_m, with h_1 = 1 for the bias term in the hidden layer. The output layer consists of outputs z_1, z_2, ..., z_k. The weights connecting the input layer to the hidden layer are represented by a matrix V of size m (d+1), where each row corresponds to the weights for a hidden unit. Similarly, the weights connecting the hidden layer to the output layer are represented by a matrix W of size k (m+1).

The activation function used in the hidden layer is often the logistic function, defined as s(v) = 1 / (1 + e^(-v)). This function can be applied component-wise to a vector v, resulting in h = s(Vx), where V is the weight matrix and x is the input vector. The output of the network is computed as z = s(Wh), where W is the weight matrix connecting the hidden layer to the output layer. This structure allows for the transformation of inputs through the hidden layer to produce outputs.

Neural networks can have multiple outputs, enabling the construction of multiple classifiers that share hidden units. One of the advantages of training multiple classifiers simultaneously is that some classifiers may benefit from useful hidden units that emerge to support others. This shared learning can enhance the overall performance of the network. Additionally, it is common to add more hidden layers for complex tasks such as image recognition, with architectures ranging from 8 to 200 hidden layers. Various configurations can be experimented with, including connections that span more than one layer.

Training usually involves stochastic or batch gradient descent. We pick a loss function L(z, y), for example, L(z, y) = ||z - y||^2, where z represents predictions and y represents true labels (which could be vectors). The cost function is defined as J(V, W) = (1/n) * Σ L(z(X), Y), where n is the number of samples. Here, Y is a matrix with one row for each sample point and one column for each output unit of the neural network. Sometimes there is just one output unit, but many neural network applications have more. Our goal is to find the weight matrices V and W that minimize J.

Typically, there are many local minima in the cost function for a neural network, and it is generally not even close to convex. Sometimes, it’s possible to end up in a bad minimum. If we start by setting all the weights to zero and then perform gradient descent on the weights, we encounter a problem. The neural network has a symmetry: there is no difference between one hidden unit and any other hidden unit. The gradient descent algorithm has no way to break this symmetry, which can lead to a situation where all the weights out of an input unit have the same value, and all the weights into an output unit have the same value.

To avoid this problem and to find a better local minimum, we start with random weights. Let w be a vector containing all the weights in V and W. In batch gradient descent, we initialize w as a vector of random weights and repeat the process of updating w using the gradient of the cost function. It is important to ensure that the random weights are not too large, as this can cause a unit"s output to get too close to zero or one, leading to "stuck' units. Stuck units tend to remain stuck, which we will discuss further in the next lecture.

Instead of batch gradient descent, we can use stochastic gradient descent, which means we use the gradient of one sample point’s loss function at each step. Typically, we shuffle the points in a random order or pick one randomly at each step. The challenging part of this algorithm is computing the gradient. If you derive one derivative for each weight, you will find that for a network with many layers of hidden units, it takes time linear in the number of edges in the neural network to compute a derivative for one weight. This is multiplied by the number of weights, leading to a significant computational cost.
Naive gradient computation takes O(edges^2) time, while backpropagation can reduce this to O(edges) time. This efficiency is crucial for training deep neural networks effectively.
Let's see what it takes to compute the gradient of an arithmetic expression. It turns into repeated applications of the chain rule from calculus. The goal is to compute f = 2 * f * 3.
Using the chain rule, we can express the derivatives as follows: @f/@d = @f/@d * @a/@d. Each value z gives a partial derivative of the form @f/@z = @f/@n computed during the forward pass.
During the backward pass, we compute the gradients using backpropagation. This involves calculating the derivatives with respect to each variable involved in the expression.

To visualize this process, draw a diagram that illustrates the flow of gradients. Start with the goal in the upper right, then include the expressions from left to right, and finally add the arrows indicating the direction of the gradient flow.
What if a unit’s output goes to more than one unit? Then we need to understand a more complicated version of the chain rule. This is a standard rule of multivariate calculus.

With this rule, let’s compute gradients for an expression from least-squares linear regression. The loss function can be expressed as L(z(τ), z(τ)) = L(z1, z2). The gradient of the loss with respect to the weights can be computed as follows: ∂L/∂w1 = ∂L/∂z1 * ∂z1/∂w1 + ∂L/∂z2 * ∂z2/∂w1.

Continuing from the previous expression, we have ∂L/∂w1 = 2(z - y) * ∂z/∂w1 + 2(z - y) * ∂z/∂w2. This shows how the loss changes with respect to the weights in the model, allowing us to update the weights during training.

Observe that we’re doing dynamic programming here. We’re computing the solutions of subproblems, then using each solution to compute the solutions of several bigger problems. This approach is essential in optimizing neural networks.

Backpropagation is a dynamic programming algorithm for computing the gradients we need to do neural network stochastic gradient descent in relation to the number of weights. Let V be a row of the weight matrix V and likewise for rows of W. Recall that s"(z) = s(z)(1 - s(z)). If h = s(Vx), then h" = s'(Vx) * x = h(1 - h) * x.

For z = s(Wh), we have z" = s"(Wh) * h = z(1 - z) * h. The derivative of z with respect to W is given by z' = z(1 - z) * h. Here is the arithmetic expression for the same neural network I drew for you three illustrations ago. It looks very different when you depict it like this, but don’t be fooled; it’s exactly the same network I started with.

Now we treat the weights V and W as the inputs, rather than the point x. The loss function L can be expressed as L = ∂L/∂z * ∂z/∂W. This can be expanded to L = ∂L/∂z * (1 - z) * h. The loss function can also be expressed as L = 1/2 * (z - y)^2, where y is the target output.

To compute the gradients, we can express L in terms of the weights V and W. The gradient with respect to V is given by ∂L/∂h = ∂L/∂z * (1 - h) * x. We compute L, L one row at a time. This process is essential for training neural networks effectively.

The vanishing gradient problem occurs when unit outputs are close to 0 or 1 for most training points, causing the gradient descent to change the weights very slowly. This results in units becoming "stuck" and leads to slow training. The more layers your network has, the more problematic this issue becomes. Most early attempts to train deep, many-layered neural networks failed due to this problem.

A common solution to the vanishing gradient problem is to replace sigmoids with ReLUs (Rectified Linear Units). The ramp function is defined as r(x) = max(0, x). While the derivative is not defined at zero, it is often treated as zero for practical purposes. Most neural networks today use ReLUs for hidden units, although it is still common to use sigmoids for output units in classification problems.

One advantage of ramp functions is that they and their gradients are very fast to compute, unlike exponentials which are slower. Even though ReLUs are linear in each half of their range, they are still nonlinear enough to compute functions like XOR easily. However, replacing sigmoids with ReLUs requires changes in the backpropagation derivation to account for the differences in gradients.

While it is rare for a ReLU"s gradient to be zero for all training data, it can happen for some training points, leading to the possibility of ReLUs getting stuck. Additionally, the output of a ReLU can be arbitrarily large, which may overwhelm downstream units. This situation is known as the "exploding gradient problem.' It is not a significant issue in shallow networks but becomes problematic in deep or recurrent networks.

Recall that we initialize a neural network with random weight values to break the symmetry between hidden units. If we make those random values too small, breaking symmetry takes a long time. But if we make them too large, we may cause the vanishing gradient problem in sigmoid units, or the exploding gradient problem in ReLUs. Here’s a rule of thumb for initializing weights into both sigmoid and ReLU units. For a unit with fan-in n, initialize each incoming edge to random weight with mean zero, std. dev. 1/sqrt(n). The idea is that the sum of all the incoming weights has mean zero and standard deviation of 1. The bigger the fan-in of a sigmoid unit, the easier it is to saturate it. So we choose smaller random initial weights for units with a bigger fan-in. We do the same with ReLUs to prevent their outputs from getting larger with every successive layer.

OUTPUT UNITS (1) Regression: usually linear output unit(s)—omit activation function. Unless you’re regressing probabilities. Usually trained with squared-error loss. If you want your regression function to sometimes be negative, clearly the output unit cannot be a ReLU or a sigmoid. For that purpose, a simple linear output unit is popular. You could say there is no activation function, or you could say that the activation function is the identity function. A linear output unit with a squared-error loss is doing least-squares linear regression on learned features (hidden units). (2) Classification: to choose from k classes, use softmax units. A set of k separate output units can do softmax regression on learned features (hidden units). E.g., in the MNIST digit recognition problem, we would have k = 10 softmax output units, one for each digit class.

Let y be a vector of labels for one training point, indicating its membership in the k classes. In the final layer, compute t = W * y and apply softmax activation to obtain prediction z. Softmax output is z_i(t) = exp(t_i) / sum(exp(t_j)) for j = 1 to k. Interpret z as an estimate of the posterior probability that the input belongs to class i. Strongly recommended: choose labels so that y_i = 1. Usually, for any single training point, people choose one label to be 1 and the others to be 0, which is called one-hot encoding. But one-hot encoding has a small disadvantage: each prediction z_i can never be exactly 1 or 0.

If you choose target labels such as 0.1 or 0.9, a neural network with lots of layers, all sufficiently wide, can "interpolate" the labels, meaning that z = y for every training point and the cost function achieves its global minimum. (Unless there are co-located training points with different labels.) From here on, we will only assume that the target labels sum to 1. To fix the vanishing gradient problem, use cross-entropy loss function instead of squared error. This method prevents the vanishing gradient problem in output units, but it can’t be applied to hidden units. For k-class softmax output, cross-entropy is L(z, y) = sum(y_i * ln(z_i)) for i = 1 to k.

Vanishing Gradients, ReLUs, Output Units and Losses, Neurobiology 103. Derivatives for k-class softmax backprop: L(z,y) = y ln(z) = y t ln(e^t_j) where i=1 to k. The loss function can be expressed as L = yW + e^t_i W e^t_j = (y - z)W. Notice that both L and L_B are relinear in the context of softmax units with cross-entropy loss. The softmax unit with cross-entropy loss does not get stuck when the softmax derivatives are small. This is related to the fact that the cross-entropy loss goes to infinity as the predicted value z approaches zero or one. The vanishing gradient of the softmax unit is compensated for by the exploding gradient of the cross-entropy loss.

Now I will show you how to perform backpropagation for ReLU hidden units, a k-class softmax output, the cross-entropy loss function, and ` regularization—which helps to reduce overfitting, just like in ridge regression. Observe that because of the simplifications we made by substituting softmax into cross-entropy, we don’t compute L explicitly, but we still have to backpropagate the value of z itself. The loss function can be expressed as L = (z - y)h + 2λW^2, where λ is the regularization parameter.

For two-class classification, softmax outputs with k = 2 are sigmoid outputs. The cross-entropy loss is L(z,y) = y ln(z) + (1 - y) ln(1 - z). You’ll recognize this as the logistic loss from logistic regression. Our derivation of the gradients for softmax units applies to sigmoid units too. You don’t necessarily have to provide the second, redundant sigmoid output z to applications, but it’s useful internally as part of computing L and L.

Cross-entropy losses are only for sigmoid and softmax outputs. For linear or ReLU outputs, cross-entropy makes no sense, but squared error loss makes sense. This distinction is important when designing neural network architectures and choosing appropriate loss functions for different types of output layers.

The field of artificial intelligence started with some wrong premises. The early AI researchers attacked problems like chess and theorem proving, because they thought those exemplified the essence of intelligence. They didn’t pay much attention at first to problems like vision and speech understanding. Any four-year-old can do those things, and so researchers underestimated their difficulty. Today, we know better. Computers can effortlessly beat four-year-olds at chess, but they still can’t play with toys well. We’ve come to realize that rule-based symbol manipulation is not the primary defining mark of intelligence. Even rats do computations that we’re hard pressed to match with our computers. We’ve also come to realize that these are different classes of problems that require very different styles of computation.

Neural networks are partly inspired by the workings of actual brains. Let’s take a look at a few things we know about biological neurons, and contrast them with both neural nets and traditional computation. CPUs are largely sequential, with nanosecond gates, and are fragile if a gate fails. They are superior for arithmetic, logical rules, and perfect key-based memory. In contrast, brains are very parallel, with millisecond neurons, and are fault-tolerant. Neurons are continually dying. You’ve probably lost a few since this lecture started, but you probably didn’t notice. This points out that our memories are stored in our brains in a diffuse representation. There is no one neuron whose death will make you forget that 2 + 2 = 4.

Artificial neural nets often share that resilience. Brains and neural nets seem to superpose memories on top of each other, all stored together in the same weights, sort of like a hologram. In the 1920s, the psychologist Karl Lashley conducted experiments to identify where in the brain memories are stored. He trained rats to run a maze, and then made lesions in different parts of the cerebral cortex, trying to erase the memory trace. Lashley failed; his rats could still find their way through the maze, no matter where he put lesions. He concluded that memories are not stored in any one area of the brain, but are distributed throughout it. Neural networks, properly trained, can duplicate this property.

By "associative memory," I mean noticing connections between things. One thing our brains are very good at is retrieving a pattern if we specify only a portion of the pattern. It’s impressive that even though a neuron needs a few milliseconds to transmit information to the next neurons downstream, we can perform very complex tasks like interpreting a visual scene in a tenth of a second. This is possible because neurons run in parallel, but also because of their computation style. Neural nets try to emulate the parallel, associative thinking style of brains, and they are the best techniques we have for many fuzzy problems, including most problems in vision and speech. Not coincidentally, neural nets are also inferior at many traditional computer tasks such as multiplying 10-digit numbers or compiling source code.

Neuron: A cell in the brain/nervous system for thinking/communication. Action potential or spike: An electrochemical impulse fired by a neuron to communicate with other neurons. Axon: The limb(s) along which the action potential propagates; "output". Most axons branch out eventually, sometimes profusely near their ends.

It turns out that squids have a very large axon they use for fast propulsion by expelling jets of water. The mathematics of action potentials was first characterized in these squid axons, and that work won a Nobel Prize in Physiology in 1963. Dendrite: Smaller limb by which a neuron receives information; "input".

Synapse: Connection from one neuron’s axon to another’s dendrite. Some synapses connect axons to muscles or glands. Neurotransmitter: Chemical released by axon terminal to stimulate dendrite. When an action potential reaches an axon terminal, it causes tiny containers of neurotransmitter, called vesicles, to empty their contents into the space where the axon terminal meets another neuron’s dendrite.

That space is called the synaptic cleft. The neurotransmitters bind to receptors on the dendrite and influence the next neuron’s body voltage. This sounds incredibly slow, but it all happens in 1 to 5 milliseconds. You have about 10^11 neurons, each with about 10^4 synapses.

Analogies between artificial neural networks and brains: The output of a neuron is not signified by voltage like the output of a transistor. The output of a neuron is the frequency at which it fires. Some neurons can fire at nearly 1,000 times a second, which you might think of as a strong "1" output. Conversely, some types of neurons can go for minutes without firing. But some types of neurons never stop firing, and for those, you might interpret a firing rate of 10 times per second as a "0".

A typical neuron is either excitatory at all its axon terminals or inhibitory at all its terminals. It can’t switch from one to the other. Artificial neural networks have an advantage here. A neuron fires when the sum of its inputs, integrated over time, reaches a high enough voltage. However, the neuron body voltage also decays slowly with time, so if the action potentials are coming in slowly enough, the neuron might not fire at all.

A neuron can’t fire more than 1,000 times a second, nor less than zero times a second. This limits its ability to overpower downstream neurons. We accomplish the same thing with the sigmoid function. Hebb’s rule (1949): "Cells that fire together, wire together." This doesn’t mean that the cells have to fire at exactly the same time. But if one cell’s firing tends to make another cell fire more often, their excitatory synaptic connection tends to grow stronger.

There are simple computer learning algorithms based on Hebb’s rule. They can work, but they’re generally not nearly as fast or effective as backpropagation. Backpropagation is one part of artificial neural networks for which the analogy is doubtful. There have been some proposals that the brain might do something vaguely like backpropagation, but it seems tenuous.

The brain is very modular. The part of our brain we think of as most characteristically human is the cerebral cortex, the seat of self-awareness, language, and abstract thinking. But the brain has a lot of other parts that take the load off the cortex. Our brainstem regulates functions like heartbeat, breathing, and sleep. Our cerebellum governs fine coordination of motor skills. When we talk about "muscle memory," much of that is in the cerebellum, and it saves us from having to consciously think about how to walk or talk or brush our teeth, so the cortex can focus on where to walk and what to say.

Our limbic system is the center of emotion and motivation, and as such, it makes a lot of the big decisions. I sometimes think that 90% of the job of our cerebral cortex is to rationalize decisions that have already been made by the limbic system.

Our visual cortex (in the occipital lobe) performs a lot of processing on the input from your eyes to change it into a more useful form. Neuroscientists and computer scientists are particularly interested in the visual cortex for several reasons. Vision is an important problem for computers. The visual cortex is one of the easier parts of the brain to study in lab animals. The visual cortex is largely a feedforward network with few neurons going backward, so it’s easier for us to train computers to behave like the visual cortex.

Although the brain has lots of specialized modules, one thing that’s interesting about the frontal lobe is that it seems to be made of general-purpose neural tissue that looks more or less the same everywhere, at least before it’s trained. If you experience damage to part of the frontal lobe early enough in life, while your brain is still growing, the functions will just relocate to healthy parts of the frontal lobe, and you’ll probably never notice the difference.

As computer scientists, our primary motivation for studying neurology is to try to get clues about how we can get computers to do tasks that humans are good at. But neurologists and psychologists have also been part of the study of neural nets from the very beginning. Their motivations are scientific: they’re curious how humans think, and how we can do the things we do.
